extracted.intended_audience: readers of Columbia Journalism Review; journalists and general public interested in media, misinformation, and media-ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A long-form magazine news feature documenting people harmed by fake news, illustrating how misinformation spreads and the consequences for victims, platforms, and institutions. Useful as a case-study style piece for journalists and media researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere amplification; investigate root causes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Don’t just hold up this guy and say 'Can you believe he thinks this?' That’s not enough. Look into why is he that way, why does he think these things, what happened to him to make him think this?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than simply showcasing extremist or conspiratorial views for spectacle, reporters should probe antecedents and motivations — examine social, psychological, and structural reasons why a source holds those beliefs. The page contrasts simple amplification with reporting that explores causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform policy and enforcement differences matter
rubrics_metrics.description: "Twitter has a much more robust end-user agreement regarding truth and transparency [than] YouTube and Facebook, [which] have been much harder."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating platforms' roles in misinformation, consider their terms of service, enforcement rigor, and responsiveness to takedown requests; platform design and rules affect how easily fake accounts and false stories persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid, proactive public communications to counter hoaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Within 24 hours, we put a release out to all the media contacts... We responded back to every single individual who reached out to us. So we tried to be as proactive and reactive as we could to nip it in the bud."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Election officials and institutions should issue timely, clear public statements and individual outreach to correct false reports and prevent escalation; proactive messaging is framed as essential crisis-management practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for the 'kernel of truth' propagation tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: "The way this propaganda works is you take something insane and wrap it in a little bit of truth, and then all those people swallow it because it’s wrapped in a little bit of truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate suspicious stories for small true elements used as credibility anchors; fact-check the claimed truths and expose how fabrications are attached to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand accountability for creators and disseminators
rubrics_metrics.description: "There has been absolutely no accountability... What is the precedent we are setting that no one got held accountable?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece stresses ethical and sometimes legal responsibility for those who create or profit from fake news (publishers, marketers, political actors). Accountability can include public apologies, job consequences, ad de-monetization, legal action, and industry sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect selective evidence and narrative-driven omission
rubrics_metrics.description: "They didn’t really have a coherent answer as to why [they say the shooting was] fake, just 'He was an actor.' But you never heard about the other 10 dads who work in finance... because that doesn’t fit their twisted narratives."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good verification looks for omitted contradictory facts and questions whether evidence is being cherry-picked to fit a preexisting narrative; reporters should surface omitted context that undermines conspiratorial claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for law-enforcement capacity and prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: "One reason law enforcement didn’t act earlier is that they’re overwhelmed. Everyone is getting threats these days. They have to prioritize."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating responses to threats and harassment stemming from fake news, consider resource constraints and triage decisions within police and federal agencies; this affects victims' recourse and the timing of intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not manufacture fake news as marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 20th Century Fox and Regency Enterprises "set up five fake local news sites... to promote A Cure for Wellness" and the campaign backfired, forcing apologies and withdrawal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing or PR that creates deceptive local-news facsimiles is unethical and risks reputational damage and harm to real local outlets; authenticity of source and clear disclosure are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use monetization controls as corrective measures
rubrics_metrics.description: "Google decided to pull ads from fake news sites in November, following Trump’s election."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ad networks and monetization policies can be leveraged to reduce incentives for producing fake-news sites; removing ad revenue is cited as an effective deterrent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Takedown and account-removal are key remediation tools
rubrics_metrics.description: "We were eventually able to close down the Twitter accounts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closing fake accounts and removing fraudulent profiles is an important response, but effectiveness varies across platforms and may require persistence and evidence from victims or institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that denials or apologies may not come and can backfire
rubrics_metrics.description: "The most outrageous spinners of hateful, horrific, and fake stories show absolutely no evidence of regret or remorse for the damage they do. On the contrary, refusing to exhibit civil decorum or own up to their lies even when confronted with irrefutable facts often bolsters their reputations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that some bad actors will double down; crafting a response strategy should account for reputation dynamics where confrontation can amplify a conspiracist's standing among followers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the psychology of conspiracy believers
rubrics_metrics.description: "It comes back to the question of brain pathology, of monological thinking... they have to feel this way, that they know something that you don’t know... They have to prove their narrative because it’s too much a part of how they identify and validate their existence on this planet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting and rebuttal strategies should be informed by the psychological drivers of belief (identity, validation, monological thinking), which can make direct factual correction ineffective for some audiences.
